title: The return
hook: lamps lit across Ayodhya; the night the whole country lights up

segments.voice: Yesterday: agni pariksha, the trial by fire, and a scene the tradition still argues about from the inside.

Fourteen years. A child born the week Rama left would be a teenager now. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana climb into the Pushpaka, the flying chariot that belonged to Ravana, and head north. As they fly, Rama points down and shows Sita everything they've been through: there's the bridge. There's where Jatayu fell. There's Kishkindha. There's the forest where we lived. And far away, in a village outside Ayodhya, a man has been waiting the whole time, sleeping on the ground, ruling with a pair of sandals on the throne. His brother Bharata.
screen: `FOURTEEN YEARS.` → `THE FLYING CHARIOT HEADS NORTH.` → `BHARATA, STILL WAITING.`

segments.voice: Rama sends Hanuman flying ahead to tell Bharata they're coming. Why send word first? Because, in the story, Bharata had made a vow: if Rama didn't come back the day the fourteen years ended, he would give up his life. And the day has come. Hanuman finds him thin, in bark clothes, hair matted, living like a hermit to match his brother in the forest. Rama is coming, Hanuman says, and Bharata's joy is so great he can hardly speak. Then the whole city pours out to meet the flying chariot, and the brothers embrace. Here's where one of the biggest festivals in the world comes in. Tradition says that when Rama came home, the people of Ayodhya lit lamps on doorsteps, on walls, along the rooftops, in every window, to welcome him and light the way home. Rows and rows of little clay lamps. In Sanskrit, a row of lamps is dipavali: dipa, a lamp, and avali, a row. Say it the way it's said all over India: Diwali. Valmiki describes Ayodhya's great celebration. The lamps, for most people, come from the way the story has been lived: every autumn, on the darkest night of the month, hundreds of millions of people light them again. Not all Hindus connect Diwali mainly with Rama; other regions tell other stories, and you'll hear some on another day. But in much of north India, this is the night. Every little clay lamp on every windowsill, every year, is that night again. You don't remember it. You repeat it. Somebody's coming home. Light the way.
screen: `HANUMAN FLIES AHEAD TO BHARATA.` · `THE BROTHERS EMBRACE.` · `DIPAVALI: A ROW OF LAMPS.` · `EVERY LAMP, EVERY YEAR, IS THIS NIGHT.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a lamp, light it; if not, turn on one small light, or just picture a clay lamp on a windowsill. Look at the flame and think of someone who's been away, a child at college, a friend who drifted, a parent far away. Picture them walking up the street at night, and your light in the window showing them where home is.
Diwali. From dipavali, a row of lamps: the night Ayodhya lit up to bring Rama home.
Your line: every lamp is this night. Ayodhya's lamps are still lit, every year. Welcome home, day sixty-nine.

howItsDone: At Diwali, on the new-moon night of the month of Kartika, Hindus light rows of clay lamps (diyas) on doorsteps, windows and rooftops; in much of north India the festival is celebrated as Rama's return to Ayodhya.

notes: Bharata's vow to enter the fire if Rama were late is in Valmiki (Ayodhya Kanda, at Chitrakoot) as remembered, and prominent in Tulsidas; confirm.

Diwali on the new-moon (amavasya) of Kartika per the purnimanta calendar (Ashvin in the amanta calendar); howItsDone says 'the month of Kartika'. Confirm.
